newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia race debate not harm Asia ties - China.
newsitem.headline: Australia race debate not harm Asia ties - China.

text.p: Chinese vice premier Zhu Rongji said on Saturday he did not believe Australia's current race debate, which has seen calls for an end to Asian immigration, would harm its relations with Asia.

Speaking at a dinner for Australian businessmen and politicians, Zhu did not mention race row politician Pauline Hanson, but said "some time ago we heard that in Australia there was some kind of opposition to immigrants from Asia".

"I think it is natural that different opinions may exist in any country, but I don't think such differences of opinion would in any way affect the historical and traditional friendship and cooperation between Australian people and people of Asian countries, including those of China," Zhu said through an interpreter.

Hanson, a former fish-and-chip shop owner who was elected an independent politician last year, has sparked a bitter race debate in Australia, calling for an end to Asian immigration and cuts to Aboriginal welfare spending.
Hanson's comments have been widely reported throughout Asia and Asian newspaper editorials have warned the Australian government it must quash racism.

Australia this week announced a big cut to 1997/98 immigration, particualrly family reunions which historically favours Asian migrants -- a move criticised by Australian politicans, business and ethnic groups.

The leader of the influential Australian Democrats Party said Prime Minister John Howard had caved in to Hanson, who opinion polls now rank as potentially the third power in domestic politics. Howard has also been widely criticised for being slow to directly confront Hanson and her policies.

Zhu arrived in Australia on Friday for a week-long landmark visit to cement improved ties and reward Canberra for an easing of its stand on human rights in China. Zhu will meet the Australian prime minister next week in Canberra.
